verses.1:
Al-Mizan defines ʿawdh as guarding oneself from harm by resorting to one able to repel it. Falq is splitting and commonly dawn, which cleaves darkness; seeking the Lord of the daybreak is thus apt for harms that cover and conceal good. It records two less likely readings: falaq as all creation, metaphorically brought from nonexistence by cleaving it apart, or as a well in hell mentioned in narrations. “What He has created” means every created thing capable of harming—human, jinn, animal, or otherwise—not that all creation is harmful.

Ghāsiq is the first darkness of night, or night after twilight has gone, and wuqūb means entering. Harm is ascribed to the entering night because darkness conceals the plots of the malevolent and leaves people more vulnerable to assault; some extend ghāsiq to anything harmful that attacks at any time. Mentioning it after the general harm emphasizes a specific danger. The three particular harms of nightfall, sorcerers, and envy share their tendency to arise while people are unaware.

The witches who blow on knots are, in the primary reading, sorceresses who bind spells through knots and blowing; women are named because they practiced it more often. Al-Mizan takes the verse, together with Hārūt and Mārūt’s account in (2:102) and Pharaoh’s magicians, to affirm that sorcery has some effect. It rejects as remote from the text the alternative that the phrase means women pressuring husbands until they weaken their opinions. Finally, the envy in (113:5) is harmful when acted upon, not merely harbored; some also include the evil eye as jealousy actualized when one sees something desirable.
